pos: n. pl. (the inhabitants of Crete, of whom Paul quotes a proverb to Titus; named once)
etymology: Greek Kretes, inhabitants of Crete; rendered Cretians by the Authorized Version at Titus 1:12.
biblical_def: The Cretians are the people of Crete, and the Authorized Version uses the form once, in a verse that has startled readers for centuries: “One of themselves, even a prophet of their own, said, The Cretians are alway liars, evil beasts, slow bellies” (Titus 1:12). Paul is quoting a Cretan poet, and then he does the thing that unsettles people: “This witness is true. Wherefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith” (Titus 1:13). He endorses the verdict. Scripture is here affirming that a people may have a real and nameable character, and that a pastor sent to them must know it. The whole point is pastoral rather than contemptuous: Paul had left Titus there precisely to build a church among such people. “For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee” (Titus 1:5). And the remedy he prescribes for a lying culture is not technique but doctrine held fast by qualified men: “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Titus 1:9). Sharp rebuke in the service of soundness in the faith — that is the apostolic method with the Cretians.

corruption_summary: Naming the real character of a culture is treated as prejudice, where Paul quotes such a verdict and says plainly that the witness is true.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reflex is that no generalisation about a people may stand, and Titus 1:12-13 breaks the rule flatly: Paul quotes a hard verdict on the Cretians and adds that it is true. He is not licensing contempt — he is in the middle of planting churches among them, and his remedy is elders, sound doctrine and sharp rebuke. A pastor who may not name what is wrong with the people he serves cannot serve them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that honest diagnosis is a work of love, and that the answer to a lying culture is the faithful word held fast by qualified men.

pos: n. pl. (Jews of Cyrene in North Africa, of the synagogue that disputed with Stephen; named once)
etymology: Greek Kyrenaioi, men of Cyrene, the Greek colony in Libya; named once in Scripture, at Acts 6:9.
biblical_def: The Cyrenians were Jews of Cyrene, the Greek city in North Africa, and they are named once, among those who took up the argument against Stephen: “Then there arose certain of the synagogue, which is called the synagogue of the Libertines, and Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of them of Cilicia and of Asia, disputing with Stephen” (Acts 6:9). This was a synagogue of the dispersion, made up of Greek-speaking Jews from across the empire, and it is sobering to note what sort of men they were: devout, well travelled, educated, and the first to move against the gospel in Jerusalem. The man they chose to debate was not a match for them: “And Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people” (Acts 6:8), and “they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake” (Acts 6:10). Unable to answer him, they procured false witnesses, and the dispute ended in a stoning: “And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59). Men of Cyrene appear again in Acts, and better: it was men of Cyprus and Cyrene who first preached the Lord Jesus to the Greeks at Antioch.

corruption_summary: Opposition to the gospel is expected from the ignorant, where Acts 6 shows it arising first from the learned and the devout.
corruption_paragraphs: The men who could not resist Stephen's wisdom were not brutes; they were the most cosmopolitan and best-educated Jews in Jerusalem, gathered in a synagogue of returned exiles from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia. When argument failed they turned to perjury and then to stones. Learning is no safeguard against enmity to Christ, and a church that assumes the educated will be more open than the simple has misread this chapter.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Stephen's opponents could not resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake, and that the Spirit's answer through an ordinary deacon silenced the best men the dispersion could field.

pos: n. pl. (Jews of Alexandria in Egypt, of the synagogue that disputed with Stephen; named once)
etymology: Greek Alexandreis, men of Alexandria, the Egyptian city founded by Alexander; named once in Scripture, at Acts 6:9.
biblical_def: The Alexandrians were Jews of Alexandria in Egypt, and they are named once, in the synagogue that argued with Stephen: “Then there arose certain of the synagogue, which is called the synagogue of the Libertines, and Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of them of Cilicia and of Asia, disputing with Stephen” (Acts 6:9). Alexandria held the largest and most learned Jewish community outside Judea. It had produced the Septuagint, and it would produce Apollos, whom Luke calls an eloquent man and mighty in the scriptures. It also produced an allegorising school of interpretation whose habits later did great damage in the church. These particular Alexandrians came to dispute and could not: “And they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake” (Acts 6:10). Stephen was a deacon appointed to serve tables, and Luke says of him: “And Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people” (Acts 6:8). What followed was not a concession but a lynching: “And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59). The best-schooled Jews of the empire met the first Christian martyr and had no answer but stones.

corruption_summary: Allegorical interpretation is treated as a richer reading of Scripture, when the Alexandrian habit of it loosened the text from its plain sense and did lasting harm.
corruption_paragraphs: Alexandria gave the church the Septuagint and also the allegorising method that would let interpreters find whatever they wished beneath the surface of the text. The Reformers recovered the plain, grammatical, historical sense as the sense — one true meaning, with legitimate application flowing from it — and the dictionary holds that recovery. Typology that Scripture itself draws is honoured; allegory that floats free of the words is not a deeper reading but a departure from reading.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Stephen, an ordinary deacon, could not be resisted by the most learned men in the dispersion, because the wisdom was not his own.

pos: n. pl. (the inhabitants of Galilee, of whom some were slaughtered by Pilate)
etymology: Greek Galilaioi, inhabitants of Galilee; the Authorized Version spells the plural Galilaeans.
biblical_def: The Galilaeans are the people of Galilee, the northern province in which the Lord was brought up and did most of His preaching. The Authorized Version uses the plural form in two notable places. The first is an atrocity: “There were present at that season some that told him of the Galilaeans, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices” (Luke 13:1). The men who reported it evidently expected the Lord to explain the victims — to say what they had done to deserve it. His answer refuses the premise and turns the question on the questioners: “Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things?” (Luke 13:2), and then “I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” (Luke 13:3). The second use is a welcome: “Then when he was come into Galilee, the Galilaeans received him, having seen all the things that he did at Jerusalem at the feast: for they also went unto the feast” (John 4:45). Galilee was despised in Jerusalem — a Galilean accent betrayed Peter in the high priest's hall — and it was in Galilee that the Christ was received.

corruption_summary: Suffering is read as a measure of the sufferer's guilt, which is precisely the reading the Lord rejects at Luke 13:2.
corruption_paragraphs: The men who brought the news about the Galilaeans wanted an account of why those particular men died, and the assumption underneath the question is that calamity sorts the wicked from the rest. The Lord denies it flatly, and then refuses to let His hearers stay in the posture of spectators: the lesson of another man's sudden death is your own repentance. Both halves must be kept. Prosperity-teaching denies the first half; a hardened fatalism ignores the second.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that calamity is a summons to repent rather than a verdict on the dead, and that the Galilee which Jerusalem despised is where the Christ was received.

pos: n. pl. (the inhabitants of Gebal, stonemasons of Phoenicia; named in the land yet to be possessed)
etymology: Hebrew Gibli, an inhabitant of Gebal, the Phoenician port the Greeks called Byblos; named at Joshua 13:5, with the Authorized Version margin offering the reading at 1 Kings 5:18.
biblical_def: The Giblites were the men of Gebal, the Phoenician port north of Beirut which the Greeks called Byblos. They are named in the survey of what Israel had not yet taken: “And the land of the Giblites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrising, from Baalgad under mount Hermon unto the entering into Hamath” (Joshua 13:5). The context is a rebuke and a promise together, spoken to an old man: “Now Joshua was old and stricken in years; and the LORD said unto him, Thou art old and stricken in years, and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed” (Joshua 13:1). God then undertakes the driving out Himself: “All the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon unto Misrephothmaim, and all the Sidonians, them will I drive out from before the children of Israel: only divide thou it by lot unto the Israelites for an inheritance, as I have commanded thee” (Joshua 13:6). Gebal was famous for its stonecutters, and the Authorized Version margin at 1 Kings 5:18 offers Giblites as the reading for the men who squared the stone for the temple: “And Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders did hew them, and the stonesquarers: so they prepared timber and stones to build the house” (1 Kings 5:18). Heathen craftsmen dressed the stone of God's house.

corruption_summary: Unfinished obedience is excused by age or circumstance, where God tells an old Joshua plainly that very much land remains to be possessed.
corruption_paragraphs: God does not soften the report for a tired man. Joshua is old, and the land is not taken, and the LORD says both things in one breath. But the burden does not fall where a reader expects: God Himself undertakes to drive out the Sidonians and the hill-country peoples, and Joshua's task is to divide by lot what God will give. Faithfulness here is not conquering everything but apportioning in faith what has been promised.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed in every generation, and that God assigns the dividing to His servants and keeps the driving out to Himself.

pos: n. pl. (men who garrisoned the towers of Tyre; named once, and of uncertain identity)
etymology: Hebrew Gammadim, of uncertain meaning; variously taken for a people, for valorous men, or from a root meaning a cubit, hence men of short stature; named once in Scripture, at Ezekiel 27:11.
biblical_def: The Gammadims are named once, in Ezekiel's lamentation over Tyre: “The men of Arvad with thine army were upon thy walls round about, and the Gammadims were in thy towers: they hanged their shields upon thy walls round about; they have made thy beauty perfect” (Ezekiel 27:11). Who they were is genuinely unknown. The Hebrew has been taken for the name of a people, for a word meaning valorous men, and for a derivative of the word for a cubit, hence men of a cubit's stature. The dictionary does not pretend to settle it. What the chapter is doing is clear enough. Ezekiel is commanded to sing a funeral song over a city still standing: “Now, thou son of man, take up a lamentation for Tyrus” (Ezekiel 27:2). Then he quotes her own boast: “O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty” (Ezekiel 27:3). The whole long inventory of her trade and her mercenaries, the Gammadims among them, exists to show what perfect beauty was made of — and what it came to: “The merchants among the people shall hiss at thee; thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt be any more” (Ezekiel 27:36). Hired shields hung on the walls made her beauty perfect, and the beauty was gone.

corruption_summary: A city's self-description is accepted as its true account, when Ezekiel quotes Tyre's boast of perfect beauty only in order to pronounce her end.
corruption_paragraphs: “I am of perfect beauty” is Tyre's own line, and Ezekiel repeats it the way a prosecutor reads a defendant's letter aloud. The inventory that follows — the fir trees, the oarsmen, the hired garrisons, the shields on the walls — is an audit, and the audit ends in hissing. A civilisation's account of itself is evidence, not verdict.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God sometimes commands a lamentation to be sung over what is still standing, and that an honest dictionary says it does not know when Scripture has not told it.

pos: n. pl. (a people descended from Mizraim, out of whom came the Philistines; spelled three ways in the Authorized Version)
etymology: Hebrew Kaphtorim, the people of Caphtor; the Authorized Version spells the name Caphthorim at 1 Chronicles 1:12, Caphtorim at Genesis 10:14, and Caphtorims at Deuteronomy 2:23.
biblical_def: The Caphthorim are a people of the table of nations, descended from Mizraim, and they appear under three spellings in the Authorized Version. The form with the h stands in Chronicles: “And Pathrusim, and Casluhim, (of whom came the Philistines,) and Caphthorim” (1 Chronicles 1:12). The parallel in Genesis spells it without: “And Pathrusim, and Casluhim, (out of whom came Philistim,) and Caphtorim” (Genesis 10:14). And Deuteronomy records what they did: “And the Avims which dwelt in Hazerim, even unto Azzah, the Caphtorims, which came forth out of Caphtor, destroyed them, and dwelt in their stead” (Deuteronomy 2:23). One people, three spellings, and a single history: they came out of Caphtor, dispossessed the Avims, and settled the coast as far as Azzah, which is Gaza. The line is traced from Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt: “And Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim” (1 Chronicles 1:11). The table of nations in Genesis 10 and 1 Chronicles 1 is the Bible's own account of how the peoples of the earth descend from the three sons of Noah, and the Philistines who would trouble Israel for centuries are placed in it by name.

corruption_summary: The table of nations is dismissed as folklore, when Scripture presents it as the account of how the peoples of the earth actually descend from Noah's three sons.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 10 and 1 Chronicles 1 are commonly handled as legendary ethnography. Scripture presents them as history, and the dictionary takes them so: one family, one flood, three sons, and from them the nations. The anthropology that follows is biblical rather than racial — all men one in Adam, all believers one in Christ — and it leaves no room for the frameworks that make race an autonomous explanation of human difference. The table of nations is the answer to those frameworks and not a casualty of them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Philistines who would afflict Israel for centuries are given a father and a homeland in God's own register of the nations.

pos: n. pl. (men of Bethlehem-Ephratah; used of Elimelech's household in the book of Ruth)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ephrathi, an inhabitant of Ephratah, the older name of Bethlehem; the plural stands once in the Authorized Version, at Ruth 1:2.
biblical_def: Ephrathites are men of Ephratah, which is Bethlehem, and the plural occurs once, naming the family that left it in a famine: “And the name of the man was Elimelech, and the name of his wife Naomi, and the name of his two sons Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites of Bethlehemjudah. And they came into the country of Moab, and continued there” (Ruth 1:2). The setting is given in the verse before: “Now it came to pass in the days when the judges ruled, that there was a famine in the land. And a certain man of Bethlehemjudah went to sojourn in the country of Moab, he, and his wife, and his two sons” (Ruth 1:1). Note what the word Ephrathite carries. These were Bethlehem people — of the town of David and of the Christ — who went to Moab for bread, and buried their men there: “And Elimelech Naomi's husband died; and she was left, and her two sons” (Ruth 1:3). The book that begins with an Ephrathite family leaving Bethlehem empty ends with a child born in Bethlehem and a line declared: “There is a son born to Naomi; and they called his name Obed: he is the father of Jesse, the father of David” (Ruth 4:17).

corruption_summary: The book of Ruth is read as a pastoral romance, when it opens with a famine, an emigration to Moab, and three graves.
corruption_paragraphs: Ruth is often handled as a gentle love story, and the first chapter will not support it. An Ephrathite family leaves the house of bread because there is no bread, settles among the people whose god was Chemosh, and loses all three of its men. The sweetness of the book is real, but it is the sweetness of redemption out of a genuine disaster, and the reader who skips the disaster has nothing left to be redeemed from.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God brought David and the Christ out of a line that had emptied itself into Moab, and that the Ephrathites who left Bethlehem in a famine are the ancestors of the Bread of Life.

pos: n. pl. (a family of the tribe of Asher, descended from Beriah; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Beri'i, the family of Beriah, whose name means in evil or in trouble; named once in Scripture, at Numbers 26:44.
biblical_def: The Beriites are a clan of Asher, named once, in the census taken in the plains of Moab: “Of the children of Asher after their families: of Jimna, the family of the Jimnites: of Jesui, the family of the Jesuites: of Beriah, the family of the Beriites” (Numbers 26:44). Their father's name means in evil or in trouble, and in the Chronicles genealogy of Ephraim another Beriah is explicitly said to have been so named because it went evil with his house. The family's own branches are given in the next verse: “Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the family of the Heberites: of Malchiel, the family of the Malchielites” (Numbers 26:45). Then the register does something it does only occasionally, and worth noticing: “And the name of the daughter of Asher was Sarah” (Numbers 26:46). A daughter in a military census. The tribe is then totalled: “These are the families of the sons of Asher according to those that were numbered of them; who were fifty and three thousand and four hundred” (Numbers 26:47). A clan whose name means trouble was numbered at better than fifty thousand.

corruption_summary: A name given out of grief is treated as a curse upon a family, where Scripture shows such a house numbered in the tens of thousands.
corruption_paragraphs: Beriah is a name given in trouble, and in the Chronicles parallel the reason is stated outright. A family founded in a grief sufficient to name a child after it was counted at fifty-three thousand four hundred by the time Israel reached the Jordan. God is not bound by the circumstances in which a household begins, and a name that records a sorrow records only the beginning of the story.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God multiplies houses founded in trouble, and that He pauses in a census of fighting men to name a daughter.

pos: n. pl. (a family of the tribe of Asher, descended from Heber son of Beriah; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Chebri, the family of Heber, whose name means a companion or one who passes over, from chabar, to join, or 'abar, to cross over; named once in Scripture, at Numbers 26:45.
biblical_def: The Heberites are a clan of Asher, named once: “Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the family of the Heberites: of Malchiel, the family of the Malchielites” (Numbers 26:45). Their father's name carries the sense of a companion or an associate, from a root meaning to join; it is also close to the root behind the word Hebrew, one who passes over. The parent clan is named in the verse before: “of Beriah, the family of the Beriites” (Numbers 26:44). This Heber of Asher is not to be confused with Heber the Kenite, whose wife Jael drove the nail through Sisera's temples, nor with Eber the ancestor of the Hebrews. The register then names a daughter — “And the name of the daughter of Asher was Sarah” (Numbers 26:46) — and totals the tribe: “These are the families of the sons of Asher according to those that were numbered of them; who were fifty and three thousand and four hundred” (Numbers 26:47). In the Chronicles genealogy of Asher the same house appears again, and the Chronicler calls its men choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. A family named for companionship furnished princes.

corruption_summary: Distinct persons bearing one name are merged by careless reading, and Scripture carries at least three men whose names are rendered Heber or Eber.
corruption_paragraphs: Heber of Asher, Heber the Kenite whose wife killed Sisera, and Eber the father of the Hebrew line are three different men, and a reader who merges them will build conclusions on sand. The dictionary names the distinction here so that the family of the Heberites is not confused with the household of Jael. Careful reading of names is not pedantry; it is the ordinary diligence the text deserves.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a clan whose name means companionship was counted among the chief of the princes, and that God numbers families by the households that actually bore the name.
